note: Curated context for the irregular migration and removals section. Numbers are from the Home Office statistics in migration.json unless a source is given. Summaries are short and conservative; follow the sources for detail.

costs.label: Home Office asylum spending, 2025-26
costs.detail: Against a budget of £3.6bn. Planned to fall to £2.4bn by 2028-29 as hotels close and backlogs clear.

costs.label: Asylum accommodation contracts, 2019-2029
costs.detail: Estimated at £4.5bn when signed in 2019. Hotels held about 35% of residents but took about 76% of the cost (£1.3bn of £1.7bn in the first seven months of 2024-25).

timeline.title: Refugee Convention
timeline.text: Defines a refugee (well-founded fear of persecution for race, religion, nationality, political opinion or social group). Article 33 forbids sending a refugee back to persecution (non-refoulement). Article 31 forbids penalising refugees for illegal entry if they come directly and present themselves promptly. The 1967 Protocol removed the time and place limits.

timeline.title: European Convention on Human Rights in force
timeline.text: The UK was the first state to ratify (1951). Article 3 (no torture or inhuman treatment) is absolute and blocks removal to a real risk of it. Article 5 limits detention. Article 8 protects private and family life and is the main ground for foreign criminals resisting deportation.

timeline.title: Immigration Act 1971
timeline.text: Still the base of UK immigration law. Created 'right of abode' for 'patrials', people with a UK-born parent or grandparent, which in practice favoured white Commonwealth citizens. Patriality was replaced by the British Nationality Act 1981; the UK Ancestry visa keeps a grandparent route for Commonwealth citizens.

timeline.title: Human Rights Act
timeline.text: Lets UK courts apply the ECHR directly. Courts must read laws compatibly where possible, or issue a declaration of incompatibility; Parliament stays sovereign.

timeline.title: Sangatte closed
timeline.text: The Red Cross centre near Calais closed after the UK and France agreed juxtaposed controls. Lorry and tunnel crossings remained the main irregular route until 2018.

timeline.title: Small boat crossings begin at scale
timeline.text: Tighter security at ports and the tunnel pushed crossings to dinghies. 299 people in 2018, 8,466 in 2020, 45,774 in 2022.

timeline.title: End of the Dublin Regulation for the UK
timeline.text: Brexit ended the UK's ability to transfer asylum seekers to the EU country they first entered. Few transfers happened under Dublin anyway (a few hundred a year).

timeline.title: Nationality and Borders Act 2022
timeline.text: Inadmissibility rules for people passing through safe countries, 'group 1 and 2' refugees, a higher bar for credibility. Over 108,000 people were considered for inadmissibility from 2021 to mid-2026; almost all were later admitted to the UK process because no country would take them.

timeline.title: Rwanda partnership announced; Albania agreement
timeline.text: April: Migration and Economic Development Partnership with Rwanda. June: the first flight was stopped by an ECtHR Rule 39 interim measure. December: a returns agreement with Albania; Albanian small boat arrivals fell from about 12,000 in 2022 to under 1,000 in 2023 and Albanians are now the largest group of enforced returns.

timeline.title: Supreme Court rules Rwanda unsafe; Illegal Migration Act
timeline.text: November 2023, R (AAA) v Home Secretary: Rwanda was not a safe third country because of the risk of onward refoulement. The Illegal Migration Act 2023 (July) imposed a duty to remove almost everyone arriving irregularly; its core duty was never brought into force because there was nowhere to remove people to.

timeline.title: Safety of Rwanda Act; scheme scrapped
timeline.text: April 2024: Parliament declared Rwanda safe by statute and disapplied parts of the HRA. Four people went voluntarily. The new government ended the scheme in July 2024 and set up a Border Security Command.

timeline.title: UK-France 'one in, one out' pilot; Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act
timeline.text: From August 2025 people arriving by small boat can be returned to France in exchange for the UK admitting the same number through a safe route. Removals under inadmissibility rose from single figures a quarter to 650 in April-June 2026. The 2025 Act gives counter-terror style powers against smuggling gangs and repeals most of the Illegal Migration Act and the Rwanda Act.

timeline.title: Asylum policy statement 'Restoring Order and Control'
timeline.text: November 2025. Refugee status becomes temporary (reviewed every 30 months), with a 20-year route to settlement for those arriving irregularly, modelled on Denmark. Consultation on 'earned settlement' raising the normal qualifying period for indefinite leave from 5 to 10 years.

timeline.title: Immigration and Asylum Bill 2026
timeline.text: Before Parliament. Creates an Independent Appeals Authority to speed appeals, narrows how Article 8 is applied, and requires some refugees to repay support (around £10,000 each, Home Office estimate).

constraints.title: Non-refoulement
constraints.law: Refugee Convention Art 33; ECHR Art 3; UN Convention Against Torture Art 3; customary international law
constraints.effect: Nobody can be sent somewhere they face persecution, torture or inhuman treatment. CAT and customary law apply even outside the ECHR.

constraints.title: Somewhere to send people
constraints.effect: The binding constraint in practice. Many small boat arrivals come from Eritrea, Sudan, Afghanistan, Iran and Syria, where returns are impossible or unsafe, and grant rates for them are high. Removal needs travel documents and the country of origin's cooperation, or a third country willing to take people.

constraints.title: Detention limits
constraints.law: Hardial Singh principles; ECHR Art 5; Immigration Act 2016 (pregnant women, adults at risk)
constraints.effect: Detention is lawful only while removal is realistic within a reasonable time. About 2,150 people were in detention at 30 June 2026 and about 21,500 left detention in the year, so each place turns over roughly ten times a year.

constraints.title: Article 8 and foreign criminals
constraints.law: ECHR Art 8; Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 Part 5A
constraints.effect: Long-resident offenders with British children or partners can resist deportation if the effect is 'unduly harsh'. Ministers want to narrow this in the 2026 Bill.

constraints.title: Modern slavery referrals
constraints.law: Modern Slavery Act 2015; Council of Europe Anti-Trafficking Convention
constraints.effect: About a fifth of small boat arrivals in 2025 had a National Referral Mechanism referral as well as an asylum claim, which pauses removal while it is decided.

constraints.title: Interim measures
constraints.effect: Strasbourg can order a pause on an individual removal; it stopped the first Rwanda flight in June 2022. The court reformed the procedure in 2023.

constraints.title: Northern Ireland
constraints.law: Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement; Windsor Framework Art 2
constraints.effect: The Agreement commits the UK to ECHR incorporation in Northern Ireland law, and Article 2 of the Windsor Framework bars any diminution of certain rights. Leaving the ECHR raises questions about both.

constraints.title: EU law enforcement cooperation
constraints.law: Trade and Cooperation Agreement Part Three, Art 692
constraints.effect: The EU may terminate police and judicial cooperation (extradition, Europol, criminal records and DNA data) if the UK denounces the ECHR.

remigration.summary: 'Remigration' is used in public debate for three different things, and the legal position differs sharply between them.

meanings.title: 1. Removing people with no right to be here
meanings.who: Mainstream government policy, and the core of the Conservative and Reform UK plans
meanings.what: Enforced and voluntary returns of refused asylum seekers, overstayers, illegal entrants and foreign national offenders. This is existing law; the debate is about scale, speed and which legal limits to change.
meanings.numbers: Total returns in the year to June 2026: about 9,700 enforced and 30,900 voluntary. The Home Office does not publish an estimate of people living in the UK without status; older estimates range from about 600,000 to 1.2 million (Pew 2017, GLA/LSE 2009 and 2020).

meanings.title: 2. Withdrawing settled status from lawful residents
meanings.who: Reform UK's September 2025 proposal to abolish indefinite leave to remain and require holders to qualify for renewable visas
meanings.what: People who were granted permanent residence lawfully would have to requalify, and those who do not would lose the right to stay. This changes the status of people who followed the rules, so it is retrospective.
meanings.numbers: About 146,000 grants of settlement in 2025 and around 200,000 in the year to June 2026. The £234bn saving Reform cited came from a Centre for Policy Studies estimate for about 800,000 likely future settlers that the CPS later withdrew (Full Fact, October 2025).

meanings.title: 3. Removing people by ethnicity or origin, including citizens
meanings.who: The sense used by parts of the European far right (for example Martin Sellner in Austria and Germany)
meanings.what: Removal or pressure to leave aimed at people of migrant background regardless of citizenship or legal status.
meanings.numbers: Unlawful under UK and international law: arbitrary deprivation of nationality, collective expulsion (ECHR Protocol 4 Art 4, which the UK has not ratified but which reflects customary law), race discrimination, and at scale potentially a crime against humanity of deportation (Rome Statute Art 7(1)(d)). The atlas covers this sense as analysis only.

points: Remove about 600,000 people who arrived or stayed illegally within one parliament (about 120,000 a year).
24,000 detention places on former military bases within 18 months; £2.5bn initial cost, excluding running costs, flights, escorts and legal costs.
Leave the ECHR, repeal the Human Rights Act, and suspend for five years the Refugee Convention, the Convention Against Torture and the anti-trafficking convention as applied in the UK.
A duty to remove anyone arriving illegally, with no asylum claims and no appeals; families and children included.
£2,500 for voluntary departure; deals with third countries; visa and aid sanctions on countries that refuse returns.

source.name: VisaVerge summary of the plan (updated April 2026)

points: Leave the ECHR and repeal the Human Rights Act, after Lord Wolfson's review concluded repeal alone would not work.
A new removals force to remove 150,000 people a year with no right to be here.
Remove people arriving illegally within a week, to their home country or a third country.
Ban asylum claims by illegal entrants; abolish the Immigration Tribunal; end immigration judicial review except on narrow grounds; abolish immigration legal aid.

source.name: Conservatives, ECHR exit policy (4 October 2025); EIN report of the conference

points: Stay in the ECHR but legislate on how Articles 3 and 8 are applied.
Temporary refugee status with 30-month reviews and a 20-year route to settlement for irregular arrivals.
Returns deals (France 'one in, one out', Iraq, the Western Balkans), visa penalties on countries that refuse returns, and hotel closures.
Faster appeals through an Independent Appeals Authority.

arithmetic: Scale: 120,000 removals a year is about 12 times the 9,700 enforced returns in the year to June 2026, and 2.6 times the most enforced and voluntary returns the UK has ever managed in a year (about 46,500 in 2013).
Detention: at about ten people through each detention place a year, 120,000 detained removals need roughly 12,000 places running full, about five to six times the number held today.

Destinations: over 70% of small boat arrivals in the year to June 2026 came from Eritrea, Sudan, Afghanistan, Somalia, Iran, Ethiopia and Syria, where enforced returns are near zero. Without receiving states, a removal duty creates people the state can neither process nor remove, as happened after the Illegal Migration Act.
Cost per removal: charter flights, escorts, detention and casework are usually put at £15,000 to £30,000 per enforced removal. The Rwanda scheme cost about £180m per person relocated.

Leaving the ECHR removes Article 3 and Article 8 claims and Rule 39 measures, but not the Refugee Convention, the Convention Against Torture, customary non-refoulement or UK judicial review on ordinary public law grounds, unless those are changed too.

law_levers.title: ECHR and the Human Rights Act
options: Repeal the Human Rights Act but stay in the ECHR
Leave the ECHR (six months' notice under Article 58)
law_levers.notes: Repealing the HRA sends cases to Strasbourg instead, which is slower but still binding. Article 15 derogation needs a public emergency threatening the life of the nation and cannot touch Article 3. Leaving removes Strasbourg but triggers the Northern Ireland, devolution and EU cooperation questions.

law_levers.title: Settlement (indefinite leave to remain)
options: Qualifying period from 5 years (current) up to 20 years
Applies to people who arrive or are granted visas after the change
law_levers.notes: Fewer people settle each year during the transition; more pay renewal fees and the health surcharge; those not settled have no recourse to public funds. Some skilled migrants leave earlier. The atlas does not model retrospective removal of status already granted.

law_levers.title: Citizenship deprivation (British Nationality Act 1981, s40)
options: Extra deprivations a year on 'conducive to the public good' grounds
law_levers.notes: The Home Secretary can deprive a person of citizenship if it is conducive to the public good and would not leave them stateless (s40(4)); people with a second nationality are exposed, sole British citizens are not. Appeals go to SIAC. Removal then depends on the other state taking them.

law_levers.title: Asylum eligibility
options: Share of irregular arrivals whose claims are declared inadmissible
law_levers.notes: Inadmissible claimants still need somewhere to go. Without returns capacity they wait in support, unable to work: the pattern after 2022 and 2023.

law_levers.title: Preferential entry by descent
options: Extra entrants a year under ancestry routes, with faster settlement
law_levers.notes: Comparators: UK Ancestry visa (Commonwealth citizens with a UK-born grandparent, five years to settlement); Ireland (citizenship by descent through a grandparent born in Ireland); Israel's Law of Return (1950); Germany's late resettler (Spätaussiedler) rules; Poland's Karta Polaka; Hungary's simplified naturalisation (2011, over a million new citizens). In UK law, Schedule 3 para 17 of the Equality Act 2010 lets ministers authorise immigration rules that distinguish by nationality or ethnic or national origins, but not by colour; East African Asians v UK (1973) found race-based entry rules could be degrading treatment under Article 3.

law_levers.title: Entry restrictions by nationality
options: Share of new visas from targeted countries blocked
Visa penalties on countries that refuse returns
law_levers.notes: Comparators: US Proclamation 9645 (2017), upheld in Trump v Hawaii (2018), and the June 2025 US ban on 12 countries; UK visa regimes and visa penalties under the 2025 Act. Knock-ons: fewer students and workers, university fee income, retaliation, and cooperation on returns, which bans tend to reduce while targeted penalties can raise it.

sentencing.title: Chemical suppression (chemical castration) for sex offenders
sentencing.text: Medication that suppresses sexual urges: SSRIs reduce intrusive sexual thoughts and anti-androgens cut testosterone. It is reversible when the drugs stop. England's voluntary pilot began in four South West prisons and was extended in September 2025 to twenty prisons in three regions, covering about 6,400 sex offenders, following the Gauke Independent Sentencing Review. Ministers have said they are considering a mandatory version.
comparators: Poland: mandatory for some child sex offenders since 2010, decided by a court before release.
Czech Republic: voluntary surgical castration was used until 2022 (criticised by the Council of Europe's anti-torture committee); hormonal treatment continues.
United States: California (1996) and several other states allow or require it for repeat child sex offenders; Louisiana added a surgical option in 2024.
Also used in Denmark, Germany (voluntary), South Korea (court-ordered since 2011), Indonesia and Kazakhstan.
sentencing.evidence: Meta-analyses (Lösel and Schmucker 2005; later reviews) find hormonal treatment among the most effective interventions for sexual reoffending among those who take it. Effects stop when medication stops, uptake under voluntary schemes is limited, and side effects include bone loss, depression and metabolic problems. There is no good evidence of an effect on non-sexual violence such as most murders.
sentencing.law: Voluntary treatment with informed consent is lawful. Compulsory treatment engages ECHR Article 3 (degrading treatment) and Article 8 (bodily integrity); the anti-torture committee has criticised compulsory or coerced schemes. Surgical castration or sterilisation as punishment is not part of the model: see the eugenics and sterilisation history.
